## 1.4 Examples

Our first set ofexamples aims to clarify in what sense the notion ofFréchet derivative relates to the various differentiation concepts you have seen in your earlier calculus courses. 

E<sub>x</sub>a<sub>mpl</sub>e 1 

[1] Let I be an open interval and $x \in I$ . The Fréchet derivative of a differentiable function $f \in \mathbb { R } ^ { I }$ at x is the linear map $t \mapsto f ^ { \prime } ( x ) t$ on R, that is, 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {f, x} (t) = f ^ {\prime} (x) t \quad \text {   for   all   } t \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

Thus the Fréchet derivative of f at x is exactly what we argued in Section 1.2 the “derivative off at $x '$ should mean. The number $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ serves only to identify the linear map a certain shift of which gives us a best approximation of f near x. 

We observe here that any differentiable function $f \in \mathbb { R } ^ { I }$ is Fréchet differentiable, and $\mathsf { D } _ { f } : I \to B ( \mathbb { R } , \mathbb { R } )$ satisfies 

$$
\mathrm{D} _ {f} (x) (t) = f ^ {\prime} (x) t \quad \text {   for   all   } x \in I \text {   and   } t \in \mathbb {R}.
$$

[2] Take any $m \in \mathbb { N }$ and any open interval I. If $\Phi : I  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x \in I$ , then $\mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x }$ is a linear operator from R into $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ given by 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (t) = (\Phi_ {1} ^ {\prime} (x) t, \ldots , \Phi_ {m} ^ {\prime} (x) t) \quad \mathrm{forall} t \in \mathbb {R},
$$

where $\Phi _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { I }$ is the ith component map of $\Phi , i = 1 , \ldots , m$ . This is a special case of a result we shall prove shortly. 

Reminder. Given any $n \in \mathbb { N }$ , let S be a subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ with nonempty interior. Where $\mathbf { e } ^ { j }$ denotes the jth unit vector in $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , the jth partial derivative of $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ at $x \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { n } } ( S )$ is defined as 

$$
\partial_ {j} \varphi (x) := \lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \left| \frac {\varphi (x + \varepsilon \mathbf {e} ^ {j}) - \varphi (x)}{\varepsilon} \right|, \quad j = 1, \ldots , n,
$$

provided that the involved limit is well-defined. If $\partial _ { j } \varphi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ exists for each $x \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( S )$ , then we call the map $x \mapsto \partial _ { j } \varphi ( x )$ on $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( S )$ the jth partial derivative of $\varphi$ . 

[3] Let $n \in \mathbb { N } ,$ , and take any open subset O of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ . As we show below, if $x \in O$ and $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { O }$ is Fréchet differentiable at x, then all partial derivatives of $\varphi$ at x exist, and we have 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) = \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \partial_ {j} \varphi (x) t _ {j} \quad \text { for   all } (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}.
$$

Thus, the Fréchet derivative of ϕ at x is none other than the linear functional that corresponds to the n-vector $( \partial _ { 1 } \varphi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) , \ldots , \partial _ { n } \varphi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) )$ ), which, as you know, is called the gradient of $\varphi$ at x. 

[4] We now generalize. Given any $m , n \in \mathbb { N }$ , let O be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and fix any $x \in O$ . Take any $\Phi _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { O } , i = 1 , \dots , m$ , and define $\Phi : { \cal O }  \mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ by 

$$
\Phi (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}) := (\Phi_ {1} (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}), \ldots , \Phi_ {m} (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n})).
$$

(Here $\Phi _ { i } \mathbf { s }$ are component maps of.) If is Fréchet differentiable at x, then the partial derivatives of each $\Phi _ { i } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { O }$ at x exist, and we have 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (t _ {1}, \ldots , t _ {n}) = \left(\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \partial_ {j} \Phi_ {1} (x) t _ {j}, \ldots , \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \partial_ {j} \Phi_ {m} (x) t _ {j}\right)
$$

$$
\text { for   all } (t _ {1}, \dots , t _ {n}) \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n},
$$

where $\partial _ { j } \Phi _ { i } ( { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ is the jth partial derivative of $\Phi _ { i }$ at $x , i = 1 , \dotsc , m , j =$ $1 , \ldots , n . ^ { 1 0 }$ Or, put differently, the linear operator $\mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x }$ satisfies 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (\gamma) = \mathbf {J} _ {\Phi} ^ {x} \gamma \quad \text { for   all } \gamma \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n},\tag{6}
$$

where $\mathrm { J } _ { \Phi } ^ { x }$ is the Jacobian matrix of  at x, that is, $\ J _ { \Phi } ^ { x } : = [ \partial _ { j } \Phi _ { i } ( x ) ] _ { m \times n }$ 

Just as $f ^ { \prime } ( x )$ in [1] turned out to be the number that identifies the Fréchet derivative off at x, here we see that the Jacobian matrix of $\Phi$ at x identifies the Fréchet derivative of at x. A certain shift ofthis operator, namely, $( \Phi ( x ) - \mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x } ( x ) ) + \mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x }$ , is an affine map from $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ into $\mathbb { R } ^ { m }$ that best approximates  near x. 

To prove (6), observe that, since $\mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x } \in \mathcal { L } ( \mathbb { R } ^ { n } , \mathbb { R } ^ { m } )$ ), there must exist a matrix $\mathbf { A } : = [ a _ { i j } ] _ { m \times n }$ with $\mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x } ( \boldsymbol { \gamma } ) = \mathbf { A } \boldsymbol { \gamma }$ for all $\gamma \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ (Example F.6). Then, by definition, 

$$
\lim _ {\omega \to x} \frac {\Phi_ {i} (\omega) - \Phi_ {i} (x) - \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} a _ {i j} (\omega_ {j} - x _ {j})}{\| \omega - x \| _ {2}} = 0, \quad i = 1, \ldots , m.
$$

It follows that 

$$
\lim _ {\varepsilon \to 0} \left| \frac {\Phi_ {i} (x + \varepsilon \mathbf {e} ^ {j}) - \Phi_ {i} (x)}{\varepsilon} - a _ {i j} \right| = 0,
$$

and hence $a _ { i j } ~ = ~ \partial _ { j } \Phi _ { i } ( { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ for each i and $j .$ That is, $\mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x } ( \gamma ) \ = \ \mathsf { J } _ { \Phi } ^ { x } \gamma$ for all $\gamma \in \mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ -

Define $\varphi : \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] \to \mathbb { R }$ by 

$$
\varphi (f) := \int_ {0} ^ {1} f (t) ^ {2} d t.
$$

Let us compute $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi }$ , which, if it exists, is a map from $\mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ into the dual of C[0, 1]. Fix any $f \in { \bf C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ , and note that 

$$
\begin{array}{c} \varphi (h) - \varphi (f) = \int_ {0} ^ {1} (h (t) ^ {2} - f (t) ^ {2}) d t \\ = 2 \int_ {0} ^ {1} f (t) (h (t) - f (t)) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {1} (h (t) - f (t)) ^ {2} d t \end{array}
$$

for any $h \in { \bf C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ . Notice that, as $\begin{array} { r } { \left\| h - f \right\| _ { \infty } \to 0 } \end{array}$ , the last term here would approach to 0 faster than $\| h - f \| _ { \infty }$  vanishes. Indeed, ifwe define $\mathbf { e } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] }$ by $\begin{array} { r } { { \bf e } ( h ) : = \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } ( h ( t ) - f ( t ) ) ^ { 2 } d t } \end{array}$ <sub>, then</sub> 

$$
\lim _ {h \to f} \left| \frac {\mathbf {e} (h)}{\left\| h - f \right\| _ {\infty}} \right| \leq \lim _ {h \to f} \left\| h - f \right\| _ {\infty} = 0.
$$

So, if we define $L \in \mathbb { R } ^ { \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] }$ by $\begin{array} { r } { L ( g ) : = 2 \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } f ( t ) g ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ , then $\varphi ( h ) = \varphi ( f ) +$ $L ( h - f ) + \mathbf { e } ( h )$ for any $h \in { \bf C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ . By Proposition 2, therefore, $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , f } = L$ Sincef was arbitrary here, we conclude that $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi } : \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] \to \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] ^ { * }$ satisfies

One-variable differential calculus is often useful in computing the Fréchet derivative ofa given function, even when the domain ofthis function is infinite-dimensional. In particular, Taylor’s Theorem is extremely useful for this purpose. Given our present purposes, all we need is the following “baby” version of that result. 

THE SECOND MEAN VALUE THEOREM
Let a and b be two distinct real numbers, and $I := co\{a, b\}$ . If $f : I \to R$ is continuously differentiable on I and twice differentiable on $\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb{R}}(I)$ , then $f(b) - f(a) = f'(a)(b - a) + \frac{1}{2} f''(c)(b - a)^2$ for some $c \in I \setminus \{a, b\}$ . 

## Proof

The idea ofthe proofis reminiscent ofthe usual way in which one deduces the Mean Value Theorem from Rol $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { e } } ^ { \prime } \boldsymbol { \mathrm { s } }$ Theorem (Exercise A.56). Define $g : I  \mathbb { R }$ by 

$$
g (t) := f (b) - f (t) - f ^ {\prime} (t) (b - t) - \frac {1}{2} M (b - t) ^ {2},
$$

where $M \in \mathbb { R }$ is chosen to guarantee that $g ( a ) = 0$ . Clearly, g is differentiable on $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } } ( I )$ , and a quick computation yields 

$$
g ^ {\prime} (t) = (b - t) \left(M - f ^ {\prime \prime} (t)\right) \quad \text {   for   any   } t \in I \backslash \{a, b \}.
$$

Moreover, since $\begin{array} { r } { g ( a ) = 0 = g ( b ) } \end{array}$ and ${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { g } } } } \in \mathbf { \mathbf { \mathbf { C } } } ^ { 1 } ( I )$ , Rolle’s Theorem guarantees that $g ^ { \prime } ( c ) = 0$ for some $c \in I \backslash \{ a , b \}$ . But then $M = f ^ { \prime \prime } ( c )$ , and we find 

$$
0 = g (a) = f (b) - f (a) - f ^ {\prime} (a) (b - a) - \frac {1}{2} f ^ {\prime \prime} (c) (b - a) ^ {2},
$$

which proves the claim.

and $\omega _ { i } ^ { * } \in c o \{ \omega _ { i } , x _ { i } \}$ for each $i = 1 , 2 , \dots$ . Consequently,

\varphi ((\omega_ {m})) - \varphi ((x _ {m})) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} u ^ {\prime} (x _ {i}) (\omega_ {i} - x _ {i}) + \frac {1}{2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {\infty} \delta^ {i} u ^ {\prime \prime} (\omega_ {i} ^ {*}) (\omega_ {i} - x _ {i}) ^ {2}\tag{7}

for any $( \omega _ { m } ) \in \ell ^ { \infty } . ^ { 1 1 }$ Again, the trick here is to notice that, as $( \omega _ { m } )  ( x _ { m } )$ the last term of this equation would approach 0 faster than $\| ( \omega _ { m } - x _ { m } ) \| _ { \infty }$ vanishes. for any $\ b ( \omega _ { m } ) \ \in \ \ b \ell ^ { \infty }$ . It follows that lim $\langle \omega _ { m } ) {  } ( x _ { m } ) \ : | \frac { { \bf e } ( ( \omega _ { m } ) ) } { \| ( \omega _ { m } - x _ { m } ) \| _ { \infty } } | = 0 ;$ , as desired. What does this mean, intuitively? Well, consider the map $\psi : \ell ^ { \infty } $ R defined by

So, the local linear behavior of $\varphi$ around $( x _ { m } )$ is best captured by the linear behavior of the affine map $\psi$ . -

Let $H \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } )$ ), and define the self-map  on $\mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ]$ by

$$

and $\theta _ { h } ( t ) \in c o \{ h ( t ) , f ( t ) \}$ for each $0 \leq t \leq 1$ . $$

so all we need here is to show that $\left\| H ^ { \prime \prime } \circ \theta _ { h } \right\| _ { \infty }$ is uniformly bounded for any h that is sufficiently close to $f$  . This is quite easy. Obviously, we have $\| \theta _ { h } \| _ { \infty } \leq \left\| f \right\| _ { \infty } + 1$ for any $h \in N _ { 1 , \mathbf { C } [ 0 , 1 ] } ( f )$ . Moreover, since $H ^ { \prime \prime }$ is contin  uous, there is a number $M > 0$ such that $\left| H ^ { \prime \prime } ( a ) \right| \leq M$ for all $a \in \mathbb { R }$ with $\begin{array} { r } { | { a } | \leq \left\| { f } \right\| _ { \infty } + 1 } \end{array}$ . Thus: 

$$
\frac {\left\| \mathbf {e} (h) \right\| _ {\infty}}{\left\| h - f \right\| _ {\infty}} \leq \frac {M}{2} \left\| h - f \right\| _ {\infty} \quad \text {   for   all   } h \in N _ {1, \mathbf {C} [ 0, 1 ]} (f).
$$

Conclusion: lim $ h \to f \ { \frac { \mathbf { e } ( h ) } { \| h - f \| _ { \infty } } } = 0$ , and (8) is true. 

Therefore, the map $g \mapsto ( H ^ { \prime } \circ f ) g$ is the best linear approximation of  near f, or, put differently, at least on a small neighborhood off, the behavior of the nonlinear operator $\Phi$ is “just like” that of the affine map $g \mapsto \left( H \circ f \right) + ( H ^ { \prime } \circ f ) ( g - f )$ -

## 1.5 Rules of Differentiation

Most of the basic rules of differentiation of one-variable calculus have straightforward generalizations in terms of Fréchet derivatives. Just as you would suspect, for instance, the Fréchet derivative of a given linear combination ofFréchet differentiable operators equals that linear combination of the Fréchet derivatives of the involved operators. 

## Proposition 3

Let X and Y be two normed linear spaces, T a subset of X, and $x \in i n t _ { X } ( T )$ Let  and  be two maps in $Y ^ { T }$ that are Fréchet differentiable at x. Then, for any real number $\alpha , \alpha \Phi + \Psi$ is Fréchet differentiable at x, and 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\alpha \Phi + \Psi , x} = \alpha \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} + \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , x}.
$$

## Proof

By Proposition 2, there exist maps $\mathbf { e } _ { \Phi }$ and $\mathbf { e } _ { \Psi }$ in $Y ^ { T }$ such that 

$$
\Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) = \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (\omega - x) + \mathbf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega) \quad \text { and }
$$

$$
\Psi (\omega) - \Psi (x) = D _ {\Psi , x} (\omega - x) + e _ {\Psi} (\omega)
$$

for all $\omega \in i n t _ { X } ( T )$ ), and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega  x } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Phi } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = 0 = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega  x } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Psi } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } } \end{array}$ . So, given any $\alpha \in \mathbb { R }$ , letting $\mathbf { e } : = \alpha \mathbf { e } _ { \Phi } + \mathbf { e } _ { \Psi }$ , we find 

$$
(\alpha \Phi (\omega) + \Psi (\omega)) - (\alpha \Phi (x) + \Psi (x)) = (\alpha D _ {\Phi , x} + D _ {\Psi , x}) (\omega - x) + e (\omega)
$$

for all $\omega \in i n t _ { X } ( T )$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array}$ . Applying Proposition 2 completes the proof. 

The next result should again be familiar from ordinary calculus. 

## Proposition 4

(The Chain Rule) Let X, Y, and Z be normed linearspaces, and let S and T be subsets of X and Y, respectively. Let $\Phi \in T ^ { S }$ and $\Psi \in Z ^ { T }$ be two maps such that  is Fréchet differentiable at $x \in i n t _ { X } ( S )$ , and at $\Phi ( x ) \in i n t _ { Y } ( T )$ Then, $\Psi \circ \Phi$ is Fréchet differentiable at x, and 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\Psi \circ \Phi , x} = \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} \circ \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x}.
$$

Proof 

By Proposition 2, there exist maps $\mathbf { e } _ { \Phi } \in Y ^ { S }$ and ${ \mathbf e } _ { \Psi } \in Z ^ { T }$ such that 

$$
\Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) = \mathrm{D} _ {\Phi , x} (\omega - x) + \mathbf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega) \quad \text {   for   all   } \omega \in i n t _ {X} (S)\tag{9}
$$

and 

$$
\Psi (w) - \Psi (\Phi (x)) = \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (w - \Phi (x)) + \mathbf {e} _ {\Psi} (w) \quad \text {   for   all   } w \in i n t _ {Y} (T),
$$

while $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { { \bf e } _ { \Phi } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = { \bf 0 } \mathrm { a n d } \operatorname* { l i m } _ { w \to \Phi ( x ) } \frac { { \bf e } _ { \Psi } ( w ) } { \| w - \Phi ( x ) \| _ { Y } } = { \bf 0 } . } \end{array}$ . It follows that, for any $\omega \in i n t _ { X } ( S )$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \Psi (\Phi (\omega)) - \Psi (\Phi (x)) & = \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x)) + \mathsf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \\ & = \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (\omega - x) + \mathsf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega)) + \mathsf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \\ & = \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} (\omega - x)) + \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\mathsf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega)) \\ & \quad + \mathsf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \\ & = \left(\mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} \circ \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x}\right) (\omega - x) + \mathsf {e} (\omega), \end{array}
$$

where $\mathbf { e } \in Z ^ { S }$ is defined as 

$$
\mathbf {e} (\omega) := \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\mathbf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega)) + \mathbf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)).
$$

By Proposition 2, therefore, it remains to show that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array}$ . To this end, observe first that 

$$
\lim _ {\omega \to x} \frac {\left\| \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} (\mathbf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega)) \right\| _ {Z}}{\| \omega - x \|} \leq \left\| \mathsf {D} _ {\Psi , \Phi (x)} \right\| ^ {*} \lim _ {\omega \to x} \frac {\left\| \mathbf {e} _ {\Phi} (\omega) \right\| _ {Y}}{\| \omega - x \|} = 0
$$

(Section J.4.3). The proof will thus be complete if we can establish that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Psi } ( \Phi ( \omega ) ) } { \left\| \omega - x \right\| } = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array}$ . This requires harder work. Note first that 

$$
\lim _ {\omega \to x} \frac {\| \mathbf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \| _ {Z}}{\| \omega - x \|} = \lim _ {\omega \to x} \left(\frac {\| \mathbf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \| _ {Z}}{\| \Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) \| _ {Y}}\right) \left(\frac {\| \Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) \| _ {Y}}{\| \omega - x \|}\right).\tag{10}
$$

But, since $\Phi$ is continuous, lim $\begin{array} { r } { \mathsf { l } _ { \mathcal { W } \to \Phi ( \mathcal { x } ) } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Psi } ( w ) } { \| w - \Phi ( \mathcal { x } ) \| _ { Y } } = 0 } \end{array}$ implies 

$$
\lim _ {\omega \to x} \frac {\| \mathbf {e} _ {\Psi} (\Phi (\omega)) \| _ {Z}}{\| \Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) \| _ {Y}} = 0.\tag{11}
$$

(Why?) Moreover, for any $\omega \in X \backslash \{ x \}$ }, (9) gives 

$$
\frac {\| \Phi (\omega) - \Phi (x) \| _ {Y}}{\| \omega - x \|} = \frac {\left\| D _ {\Phi , x} (\omega - x) + e _ {\Phi} (\omega) \right\| _ {Y}}{\| \omega - x \|} \leq \left\| D _ {\Phi , x} \right\| ^ {*} + \frac {\| e _ {\Phi} (\omega) \| _ {Y}}{\| \omega - x \|}.
$$

(Why?) Since $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Phi } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = \mathbf { 0 } } \end{array}$ , therefore, there exists an $\varepsilon \ > \ 0$ such that $\begin{array} { r l r } { \frac { \| \Phi ( \omega ) - \Phi ( x ) \| _ { Y } } { \| \omega - x \| } \leq } & { { } \big \| \mathsf { D } _ { \Phi , x } \big \| ^ { * } + 1 } \end{array}$ for all $\omega \in \ N _ { \varepsilon , X } ( x ) \backslash \{ x \}$ . Combining  <sub>this observation with (11) and (10) yields</sub> $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } _ { \Psi } ( \Phi ( \omega ) ) } { \left\| \omega - x \right\| } = 0 } \end{array}$ , as we sought.  

Here is a quick illustration of how such rules of differentiation are used in practice.

## 1.6 The Second Fréchet Derivative of a Real Function

To outline a basic introduction to optimization theory, we also need to go through the notion of the second Fréchet derivative of real functions. Just as in ordinary calculus, the idea is to define this notion as the derivative of the derivative. Unfortunately, life gets a bit complicated here. Recall that the Fréchet derivative $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi }$ of a real function $\varphi$ defined on an open subset O of a normed linear space X is a function that maps O into $X ^ { * }$ . Therefore, the Fréchet derivative of $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi }$ at $x \in O$ is a continuous linear function that maps X into $X ^ { * }$ . Put differently, the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at $_ x$ is a member of $B ( X , X ^ { * } )$ 

In case you find this confusing, let us see how this situation compares with differentiating a function of the form $\varphi : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }  \mathbb { R }$ twice. In calculus, by the derivative ofϕ at $\boldsymbol { x } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , we understand the gradient of $\dot { \varphi } _ { ; }$ , that is, the vector $( \partial _ { 1 } \varphi ( x ) , \partial _ { 2 } \varphi ( x ) ) \in \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ . In turn, the second derivative of $\varphi$ at x is the matrix $\mathbf { H } ^ { x } : = [ \partial _ { i j } \varphi ( x ) ] _ { 2 \times 2 }$ , where by $\partial _ { i j } \varphi ( x )$ , we understand $\partial _ { i } \partial _ { j } \varphi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } )$ . (You might recall that this matrix is called the Hessian of ϕ at x.) Given Example 1.[3], it is only natural that the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at $_ { x }$ is the linear operator induced by the matrix $\mathbf { H } ^ { x } \ ( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } \gamma \mapsto \mathbf { { H } } ^ { x } \gamma )$ and hence it is a linear function that maps $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ into $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ . Since the dual of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ is $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ (Example J.7), this situation conforms perfectly with the outline of the previous paragraph. 

Things will become clearer later. Let us first state the definition of the second Fréchet derivative of a real function formally. 

DEFINITION
Let T be a nonempty subset of a normed linear space X and $\varphi: T \to R$ a Fréchet differentiable map. For any given $x \in int_{X}(T)$ , if $D_{\varphi}: int_{X}(T) \to X^{*}$ is Fréchet differentiable at x, then we say that $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable at x. In this case, the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at x, denoted by $D_{\varphi,x}^{2}$ , is a member of $\mathcal{B}(X, X^{*})$ ; we define $D_{\varphi,x}^{2} := D_{D_{\varphi,x}}$ .

If O is a nonempty open subset of X with $O \subseteq T$ , and if $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable at every $x \in O$ , then we say that $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable on O. If $O = int_{X}(T)$ here, then $\varphi$ is said to be twice Fréchet differentiable. 

The thing to get used to here is that $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } \in B ( X , X ^ { \ast } )$ , that is, $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ( \gamma ) \in X ^ { * }$ for each $\gamma \in X$ . We should thus write $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ( \gamma ) ( z )$ for the value of the linear functional $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ( \boldsymbol { \gamma } )$ at z. It is, however, customary to write $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ( \gamma , z )$ instead of $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ( \gamma ) ( z )$ , thereby thinking of $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 }$ as a function that maps $X \times X$ into R. From this viewpoint, $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 }$ is a continuous bilinear functional on $X \times X$ (Exercise J.52).<sup>12</sup> 

The following is an analogue (and an easy consequence) of Proposition 2 for the second Fréchet derivative of a real function. 

## P<sub>r</sub>o<sub>p</sub>os<sub>i</sub>t<sub>i</sub>o<sub>n</sub> 5

Let X be a normed linear space, T a subset of $X , x \in i n t _ { X } ( T )$ , and $L \in$ $B ( X , X ^ { * } )$ . For any $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { T }$ , L is the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at $x i f ,$ and only if, there exists a continuous map $\mathbf { e } : T  X ^ { * }$ such that 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , \omega} = \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} + L (\omega - x) + \mathbf {e} (\omega) \quad f o r a l l \omega \in i n t _ {X} (T),
$$

and $\operatorname* { l i m } _ { \omega \to x } \frac { \mathbf { e } ( \omega ) } { \| \omega - x \| } = \mathbf { 0 } .$

[2] Given any $n \in \mathbb { N } ,$ , let O be an open subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ , and take any Fréchet differentiable map $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { O }$ . If $\dot { \varphi }$ is twice Fréchet differentiable at $x \in O _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , then all second-order partial derivatives o $\dot { \varphi }$ at x exist, and we have 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} ^ {2} (u, v) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \partial_ {i j} \varphi (x) u _ {i} v _ {j} \quad \text { for   all } u, v \in \mathbb {R} ^ {n}.
$$

Thus, the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at x is none other than the symmetric bilinear functional induced by the so-called Hessian matrix $[ \partial _ { i j } \varphi ( { \boldsymbol { x } } ) ] _ { n \times n }$ of $\varphi$ at x. -

## 1.7 Differentiation on Relatively Open Sets

We have now at hand a potent theory ofdifferentiation that generalizes the classic theory. There still remains one major difficulty, however. Insofar as our basic definition is concerned, we are unable to differentiate a map that is defined on a subset ofa normed linear space with no interior. For instance, let $S = \{ ( a , 1 ) : 0 < a < 1 \}$ , and define $\varphi : S  \mathbb { R }$ by $\varphi ( a , 1 ) : = a ^ { 2 } .$ What is the Fréchet derivative of $\varphi \colon$ Well, since S has no interior in $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } ,$ our basic definition does not even allow us to pose this question. That definition is based on the idea ofperturbing (infinitesimally) a given point in the interior ofthe domain of a map in any direction in the space, and analyzing the behavior ofthe resulting difference-quotient. In this example, because $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( S ) = \varnothing$ we cannot proceed in this manner. Indeed, the variations we consider must be horizontal in this case. Put differently, ${ \mathrm { i f } } \ x \in S$ and we wish to study the difference-quotient $\frac { \varphi ( \omega ) - \varphi ( x ) } { \omega - x }$ , the variation $\omega - x$ must belong to the linear subspace $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ . So, in this example, the Fréchet derivative o $\cdot _ { \varphi }$ needs to be viewed as a linear functional from $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ into R (and not from $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ into R). 

Apparently, there is an obvious way we can generalize the definition of the Fréchet derivative and capture these sorts of examples. All we need is to take the domain of the function to be differentiated as open in the affine manifold it generates. Let us first give such sets a name. 

DEFINITION
Let X be a normed linear space. A subset S of X is said to be relatively open if $|S| > 1$ and S is open in $aff(S)$ . $^{13}$ 

Now consider a real map ϕ whose domain S is relatively open in some normed linear space. Obviously, the difference-quotient $\frac { \varphi ( \omega ) - \varphi ( x ) } { \omega - x }$ makes sense iff $\omega \in S \backslash \{ x \}$ . Therefore, span $( S - x )$ is the linear space that contains all possible variations about x, or equivalently, $a f f ( S )$ is the set ofall possible directions of perturbing x. (Recall the example considered above.) We are therefore led to define the Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at x as a bounded linear functional on span $( S - x )$ 

Notation. Let T be a subset of a normed linear space. In what follows we denote the interior of T in $a f ( T )$ as $T ^ { \diamondsuit }$ , that is, 

$$
T ^ {\diamond} := i n t _ {a f f (T)} (T).
$$

Thus, T is relatively open iff $T = T ^ { \diamond }$ . Moreover, span $( T ^ { \diamond } - z ) = s p a n ( T - z )$ for any $z ~ \in ~ T ^ { \circ } , { } ^ { 1 4 }$ and if T is convex and $T ^ { \diamondsuit } \neq \emptyset$ , then $T ^ { \diamond } = r i ( T )$ (Proposition I.11). 

DEFINITION
Let X and Y be two normed linear spaces and T a subset of X with $|T| > 1$ and $T^{\diamond} \neq \emptyset$ .¹⁵ Let $\mathbf{s}(T) := \text{span}(T - z)$ (13)

where $z \in T^{\diamond}$ is arbitrary.¹⁶ For any $x \in T^{\diamond}$ , a map $\Phi : T \to Y$ is said to be Fréchet differentiable at x if there is a continuous linear operator $D_{\Phi,x} \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{s}(T), Y)$ such that $\lim_{\omega \to x} \frac{\Phi(\omega) - \Phi(x) - D_{\Phi,x}(\omega - x)}{\|\omega - x\|} = 0.$ The linear operator $D_{\Phi,x}$ is called the Fréchet derivative of $\Phi$ at x.

If $\Phi$ is Fréchet differentiable at every $x \in T^{\diamond}$ , then we say that $\Phi$ is Fréchet differentiable. In this case, we say that $\Phi$ is continuously Fréchet differentiable if the map $D_{\Phi} : T^{\diamond} \to \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{s}(T), Y)$ , defined by $D_{\Phi}(x) := D_{\Phi,x}$ , is continuous. 

## Definition

Let T be a subset of a normed linear space X with $\vert T \vert > 1$ and $T ^ { \diamondsuit } \neq$ $\varnothing ,$ and take a Fréchet differentiable map $\varphi : T  \mathbb { R }$ . For any given $x \in T ^ { \diamond } ,$ , if $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi } : T ^ { \diamond } \to \mathbf { s } ( T ) ^ { * }$ is Fréchet differentiable at x (where $\mathbf { s } ( T )$ is defined by (13)), we say that $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable at x. In this case, the second Fréchet derivative of $\varphi$ at $x ,$ , denoted by $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } ,$ is a member of $\mathcal { B } ( \mathbf { s } ( T ) , \mathbf { s } ( T ) ^ { * } )$ ; we define $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } ^ { 2 } : = \mathsf { D } _ { \mathsf { D } _ { \varphi } , x }$ . If $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable at every $x \in T ^ { \diamond }$ , then we say that $\varphi$ is twice Fréchet differentiable. 

These definitions extend the ones given in Sections 1.3 and 1.6. After all, if $T$ is a subset of X with $i n t _ { X } ( T ) \neq \varnothing .$ , then $a f f ( T ) = X = \mathbf { s } ( T ) { \mathrm { - y e s ? - s o } }$ the two definitions become identical. Moreover, most ofour findings in the previous sections apply to the Fréchet derivatives of maps defined on any nonsingleton $T \subseteq X$ with $T ^ { \diamondsuit } \neq \varnothing$ . All we have to do is apply those results on $\mathbf { s } ( T )$ as opposed to $X . ^ { 1 7 }$ For instance, Proposition 2 becomes the following in this setup. 

PROPOSITION 2* Let $X$ and $Y$ be two normed linear spaces, $T$ a subset of $X$ , $x \in T^{\diamond}$ , and $L \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbf{s}(T), Y)$ , where $\mathbf{s}(T)$ is defined by (13). For any $\Phi \in Y^{T}$ , $L$ is the Fréchet derivative of $\Phi$ at $x$ if, and only if, there exists a continuous map $\mathbf{e} \in Y^{T}$ such that $\Phi(\omega) = \Phi(x) + L(\omega - x) + \mathbf{e}(\omega)$ for all $\omega \in T^{\diamond}$ , and $\lim_{\omega \to x} \frac{\mathbf{e}(\omega)}{\|\omega - x\|} = \mathbf{0}$ . 

Let us now go back to our silly little example in which the question was to find the Fréchet derivative of $\varphi : S  \mathbb { R }$ where $S = \{ ( a , 1 ) : 0 < a < 1 \}$ } and $\varphi ( a , 1 ) : = a ^ { 2 }$ . As S is relatively open, this question now makes sense. Besides, it is very easy to answer. For any $0 < a < 1 , \mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , ( a , 1 ) }$ is a linear functional on $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ , and just as one would like to see, we have $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , ( a , 1 ) } ( t , 0 ) = 2 a t$ for any $t \in \mathbb { R }$ . Moreover, $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , ( a , 1 ) } ^ { 2 }$ is a linear operator from $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ into the dual of $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ (which is $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ itself ), or equivalently, a bilinear functional on $( \mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \} ) \times ( \mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \} )$ ). We have: 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , (a, 1)} ^ {2} ((u, 0), (v, 0)) = 2 u v \quad \text { for   all } u, v \in \mathbb {R},
$$

as you can easily check.<sup>18</sup> 

Remark 1. Not only that the definitions we have given in this section reduce to those of the earlier sections for maps defined on sets with nonempty interior, they are also consistent with them in the following sense. Let X and Y be two normed linear spaces, and $S \subseteq X$ . Suppose that $\Phi : S  Y$ is 

Fréchet differentiable at $x \in i n t _ { X } ( S )$ . Then, for any $T \subseteq S$ with $\vert T \vert > 1$ and $x \in T ^ { \diamond }$ , the map $\Phi | _ { T }$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x ,$ , and we have 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\Phi | _ {T}, x} = \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , x} | _ {\mathbf {s} (T)}.
$$

The proof is straightforward. 

## 2 Generalizations of the Mean Value Theorem

## 2.1 The Generalized Mean Value Theorem

One way ofstating the classic Mean Value Theorem is the following: Given a differentiable real mapf on an open interval I, for any a, $b \in I$ with $a < b ,$ there exists a $c \in ( a , b )$ such that $f ( b ) - f ( a ) = f ^ { \prime } ( c ) ( b - a )$ . This fact extends readily to real maps defined on a normed linear space. 

THE GENERALIZED MEAN VALUE THEOREM
Let S be a relatively open and convex subset of a normed linear space X and $\varphi \in R^{S}$ a Fréchet differentiable map. Then, for any distinct $x, y \in S$ , $\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)=D_{\varphi,z}(x-\gamma)$ for some $z \in co\{x, y\} \setminus \{x, y\}$ . 

Notice that the entire action takes place on the line segment co $\{ x , \gamma \}$ here. Intuitively speaking, then, we should be able to prove this result simply by applying the good ol’ Mean Value Theorem on this line segment. The following elementary observation, which generalizes the result found in Exercise 22, is a means to this end.

Proof

## 2.2<sup>∗</sup> The Mean Value Inequality

We noted above that the Generalized Mean Value Theorem need not apply to maps that are not real-valued. It turns out that this is not a major difficulty. Indeed, most of the results of one-variable calculus that can be deduced from the Mean Value Theorem can also be obtained by using the so-called Mean Value Inequality: If O is an open subset of R that contains the open interval (a, b), and $f \in \mathbb { R } ^ { O }$ is differentiable, then 

$$
f (b) - f (a) \leq \sup \left\{\left| f ^ {\prime} (t) \right|: t \in O \right\} (b - a).
$$

Fortunately, this result extends nicely to the present framework, and this extension is all one needs for most purposes.<sup>22</sup> 

Let X and Y be two normed linear spaces and O a nonempty open subset of X. Let $\Phi \in Y ^ { O }$ be Fréchet differentiable. Then, for every $x , \gamma \in O$ with $c o \{ x , \gamma \} \subseteq O$ , there exists a real number $K \geq 0$ such that 

$$
\left\| \Phi (x) - \Phi (\gamma) \right\| _ {Y} \leq K \left\| x - \gamma \right\|.\tag{14}
$$

In particular, if 

$$
K \geq \sup \left\{\left\| \mathsf {D} _ {\Phi , w} \right\| ^ {*}: w \in c o \{x, \gamma \} \right\},\tag{15}
$$

then (14) holds. 

The method ofproofthat we will use to establish this result is one we have already used a good number of times, the method of “butterfly hunting.” (Recall the proof of the Heine-Borel Theorem, for example.) We will proceed by assuming that the claim is not true, and then make a suitable nestedinterval argument to derive a contradiction. The following elementary fact will be used in this argument. 

## Lemma 2

$H f x , \gamma ,$ , and $z a r e$ any points in a normed linear space with $z \in c o \{ x , \gamma \}$ , then 

$$
\left\| x - \gamma \right\| = \left\| x - z \right\| + \left\| z - \gamma \right\|.
$$

## Proof

By hypothesis, there exists a $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ such that $z = \lambda x + ( 1 - \lambda ) \gamma$ . Then $x - z = ( 1 - \lambda ) ( x - \gamma )$ and $z - \gamma = \lambda ( x - \gamma )$ ). Thus 

$$
\left\| x - z \right\| + \left\| z - \gamma \right\| = (1 - \lambda) \left\| x - \gamma \right\| + \lambda \left\| x - \gamma \right\| = \left\| x - \gamma \right\|,
$$

as we sought. 

## Proof of the Mean Value Ine<sub>q</sub>uality

Fix any $x , \gamma \in { \cal O }$ with $c o \{ x , \gamma \} \ \subseteq { \cal { O } } _ { \mathrm { { i } } }$ , and take any $K \ge 0$ that satisfies $( 1 5 ) . ^ { 2 3 }$ Toward deriving a contradiction, suppose that there exists an $\varepsilon > 0$ such that 

$$
\left\| \Phi (x) - \Phi (\gamma) \right\| _ {Y} > (K + \varepsilon) \left\| x - \gamma \right\|.
$$

Let $x ^ { 0 } : = x$ and $\gamma ^ { 0 } : = \gamma$ . Since, by subadditivity of $\left\| \cdot \right\| _ { Y }$ 

$$
\left\| \Phi (x) - \Phi \left(\frac {1}{2} x + \frac {1}{2} \gamma\right) \right\| _ {Y} + \left\| \Phi \left(\frac {1}{2} x + \frac {1}{2} \gamma\right) - \Phi (\gamma) \right\| _ {Y} > (K + \varepsilon) \left\| x - \gamma \right\|,
$$

either $\begin{array} { r } { \left\| \Phi ( x ) - \Phi \left( \frac { 1 } { 2 } x + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \gamma \right) \right\| _ { Y } \mathrm { o r } \left\| \Phi \left( \frac { 1 } { 2 } x + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \gamma \right) - \Phi ( \gamma ) \right\| _ { Y } } \end{array}$ must be strictly greater than ${ \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ( K + \varepsilon ) \left\| x - \gamma \right\|$  . If the former case holds, let $\boldsymbol { x } ^ { 1 } : = \boldsymbol { x } ^ { 0 }$ and $\gamma ^ { 1 } : = \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } x + \frac { 1 } { 2 } \gamma$  , and otherwise let $x ^ { 1 } : = { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } x + { \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } } \gamma$ and $\gamma ^ { 1 } : = \gamma ^ { 0 } .$ Either way we have $\left\| \Phi ( x ^ { 1 } ) - \Phi ( \gamma ^ { 1 } ) \right\| _ { Y } > ( K + \varepsilon ) \left\| x ^ { 1 } - \gamma ^ { 1 } \right\|$ . Proceeding this way inductively, we obtain two sequences $( x ^ { m } )$ and $( \gamma ^ { m } )$ in $c o \{ x , \gamma \}$ and a vector $z \in c o \{ x , \gamma \}$ with the following properties: For all $m \in \mathbb { N }$ 

(i) $z \in c o \{ x ^ { m } , \gamma ^ { m } \}$

## 3 Fréchet Differentiation and Concave Maps

## 3.1 Remarks on the Differentiability of Concave Maps

You might recall that a concave function f defined on an open interval I possesses very nice differentiability properties. In particular, any such f is differentiable everywhere on I but countably many points. Although our main goal is to study those concave functions that are defined on convex subsets of an arbitrary normed linear space, it may still be a good idea to warm up by sketching a quick proof of this elementary fact. 

## E<sub>x</sub>a<sub>mpl</sub>e 9

Let I be an open interval and $f \in \mathbb { R } ^ { I }$ a concave map. It is easy to check that the right-derivative $f _ { + } ^ { \prime }$ off is a well-defined and decreasing function on I. (Prove!) Thus if $( x _ { m } ) \in I ^ { \infty }$ is a decreasing sequence with $x _ { m } \searrow x$ , we have lim $f _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( x _ { m } ) \leq f _ { + } ^ { \prime } ( x )$ . On the other hand, concavity implies that 

$$
f _ {+} ^ {\prime} (x _ {m}) \geq \frac {f (\gamma) - f (x _ {m})}{\gamma - x _ {m}} \quad \mathrm{forall} \gamma \in I \mathrm{with} \gamma > x _ {m},
$$

for each m, so, since f is continuous (Corollary A.2), we get 

$$
\lim f _ {+} ^ {\prime} (x _ {m}) \geq \frac {f (\gamma) - f (x)}{\gamma - x} \quad \text {   for   all   } \gamma \in I \text {   with   } \gamma > x.
$$

Conclusion: $f$ is differentiable at $x \ \mathrm { i f f } \ f _ { + } ^ { \prime }$ is continuous at x. But since $f _ { + }$ is a monotonic function, it can have at most countably many points of discontinuity (Exercise B.8). Therefore, $\mathrm { . } f$ is differentiable everywhere on I but countably many points. -

For instance, the map $\varphi : \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }  \mathbb { R }$ defined by $\varphi ( u , v ) : = - | u |$ is a concave function that is not differentiable on the uncountable set $\mathbb { R } \times \{ 0 \}$ Worse still, a concave function on an infinite-dimensional normed linear space may not possess a Fréchet derivative anywhere! Nevertheless, the concave functions that arise in most economic applications are in fact continuously differentiable, and hence for most practical purposes, these observations are not too problematic.

## 3.2 Fréchet Differentiable Concave Maps

Recall that there are various useful ways of characterizing the concavity of differentiable real maps defined on an open interval. It is more than likely that you are familiar with the fact that if I is an open interval and $\boldsymbol { \varphi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { I }$ is differentiable and concave, then the difference-quotient $\frac { \varphi ( \gamma ) - \varphi ( x ) } { \gamma - x }$ is less than $\varphi ^ { \prime } ( x )$ if $\gamma > x$ , while it exceeds $\varphi ^ { \prime } ( x )$ if $x > \gamma$ . (Draw a picture.) Put more concisely, 

$$
\varphi (\gamma) - \varphi (x) \leq \varphi^ {\prime} (x) (\gamma - x) \quad \text {   for   all   } x, \gamma \in I.
$$

A useful consequence of this observation is that a differentiable $\boldsymbol \varphi \in \mathbb R ^ { I }$ is concave iffits derivative is a decreasing function on I. We now extend these facts to the context of real maps defined on open and convex subsets of an arbitrary normed linear space. 

Proposition 6 

Let S be a relatively open and convex subset of a normed linear space and $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { S }$ a Fréchet differentiable map. Then, $\varphi$ is concave $i f ,$ and only if, 

$$
\varphi (\gamma) - \varphi (x) \leq \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} (\gamma - x) \quad f o r a l l x, \gamma \in S.\tag{16}
$$

Proof 

Suppose that $\varphi$ is concave, and take any $x , \gamma \in S$ . Then, 

$$
\varphi (x + \lambda (\gamma - x)) = \varphi ((1 - \lambda) x + \lambda \gamma) \geq (1 - \lambda) \varphi (x) + \lambda \varphi (\gamma)
$$

for all $0 \leq \lambda \leq 1$ . Thus 

$$
\frac {1}{\lambda} \left(\varphi (x + \lambda (\gamma - x)) - \varphi (x) - \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} (\lambda (\gamma - x))\right) \geq \varphi (\gamma) - \varphi (x) - \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x} (\gamma - x)
$$

for each $0 < \lambda < 1$ . We obtain (16) by letting $\lambda \to 0$ in this expression, and using the definition of $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x } . ^ { 2 7 }$ 

Conversely, suppose (16) is true. Take any $x , \gamma \in S$ and $0 < \lambda < 1$ . If we set $z : = \lambda x + ( 1 - \lambda ) \gamma$ , then $\lambda ( x - z ) + ( 1 - \lambda ) ( \gamma - z ) = 0 ,$ so (16) implies 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \varphi (z) = \lambda \varphi (z) + (1 - \lambda) \varphi (z) + \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , z} (\lambda (x - z) + (1 - \lambda) (\gamma - z)) \\ \qquad = \lambda (\varphi (z) + \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , z} (x - z)) + (1 - \lambda) (\varphi (z) + \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , z} (\gamma - z)) \\ \qquad \geq \lambda \varphi (x) + (1 - \lambda) \varphi (\gamma), \end{array}
$$

as we sought.

But a differentiable real function on a given open interval is decreasing iff its derivative is not strictly positive anywhere on that interval. It follows that a twice differentiable real map on an open interval is concave iffthe second derivative of that map is less than zero everywhere. You of course know that the derivative of a differentiable real map need not be continuous. (That is, a differentiable real function need not be continuously differentiable.) One of the remarkable properties of concave (and hence convex) real functions defined on an open interval is that their differentiability implies their continuous differentiability. (Go back and reexamine Example 9—we proved this fact there.) As it happens, this observation generalizes to our present setting as well. Indeed, for concave real maps on a normed linear space, the notions ofFréchet differentiability and continuous Fréchet differentiability coincide.

We conclude this section with a few preliminary remarks about the notion of the superdifferential of a real map. Although this concept is useful in the theory of nonsmooth optimization, we will not need it in the rest of our treatment, so our discussion proceeds only in terms of a few exercises. 

DEFINITION
Let O be a nonempty open subset of a normed linear space X and $\varphi \in R^{O}$ . We say that a continuous linear functional $L \in X^{*}$ is a supergradient of $\varphi$ at $x \in O$ if $\varphi(\omega) \leq \varphi(x) + L(\omega - x)$ for all $\omega \in O$ .
The set of all supergradients of $\varphi$ at x is called the superdifferential of $\varphi$ at x, and is denoted by $\partial\varphi(x)$ . 

Geometrically speaking, L is a supergradient ofϕ at x iffthe hyperplane $H _ { L } : = \{ ( \omega , t ) \in X \times \mathbb { R } : L ( \omega - x ) - t = - \varphi ( x ) \}$ lies above the graph of $\varphi .$ . Since $( x , \varphi ( x ) )$ is on this hyperplane, we can therefore say that L is a supergradient of $\dot { \varphi }$ at x iff $H _ { L }$ supports the set $\{ ( \omega , t ) : \varphi ( \omega ) \geq t \} \mathrm { a t } \left( x , \varphi ( x ) \right)$ (Recall that the latter set is called the hypograph of ϕ.) In turn, ∂ϕ(x) equals the set of all L such that $H _ { L }$ supports the hypograph ofϕ at $( x , \varphi ( x ) )$

## 4 Optimization

Classical differential calculus provides powerful methods for optimizing a given real function of finitely many variables. Indeed, students of formal economics are bound to be big fans of the (informal) rule, “equate the first derivative of the objective function to zero and solve for the independent variables.” The general theory ofcalculus we have developed in this chapter can be used in much the same way. Here is how. 

## 4.1 Local Extrema of Real Maps

Let us begin by recalling the following standard terminology ofoptimization theory. 

## Definition

Let S be a nonempty subset ofa normed linear space $X ,$ , and $\varphi$ a real map on S. We say that a point $x ^ { * }$ in S is a local maximum of $\varphi$ if 

$$
\varphi (x ^ {*}) \geq \varphi (N _ {\delta , X} (x ^ {*}) \cap S) \quad \text {   for   some   } \delta > 0,
$$

and a global maximum of $\varphi$ if 

$$
\varphi (x ^ {*}) \geq \varphi (S).
$$

In turn, $x ^ { * }$ is a local (global) minimum of $\varphi$ if it is a local (global) maximum of $- \varphi$ . By a local (global) extremum of $\varphi _ { ; }$ , we mean a point in S that is either a local (global) maximum or local (global) minimum of $\varphi .$ . 

## Definition

Let T be a subset of a normed linear space X and $\varphi$ a real map on $T . ^ { 3 0 }$ We say that a point $x ^ { * } \in T ^ { \diamond }$ is a stationary point of ϕ if $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x ^ { * } }$ is the zero functional on span $( T - x ^ { * } )$ ), that is, 

$$
\mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , x ^ {*}} (x) = 0 \quad \text { for   all } x \in s p a n (T - x ^ {*}).
$$

The rule “to maximize (or minimize) a given function, equate its first derivative to zero, and solve for the independent variable(s)” can thus be reworded as “to maximize (or minimize) a given function, find its stationary points.” Or, put formally, we have the following. 

## Proposition 8

Let T be a nonempty subset ofa normed linearspace X, $x ^ { * } \in T ^ { \diamond } ,$ , and $\boldsymbol { \varphi } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { T }$ If $\varphi$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x ^ { * }$ and $x ^ { * }$ is a local extremum of $\varphi _ { : }$ , then $x ^ { * }$ is a stationary point of $\varphi .$ . 

## Proof

Assume that $\varphi$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x ^ { * }$ , and without loss of generality, let $x ^ { * }$ be a local maximum of $\varphi .$ . To derive a contradiction, suppose $\mathsf { D } _ { \varphi , x ^ { * } } ( x ) > 0$ for some $x \in s p a n ( T - x ^ { * } ) . ^ { 3 1 }$ (Obviously, $x \neq \mathbf { 0 . } )$ Now define $\omega _ { \lambda } : = x ^ { * } + \lambda x$ for any $\lambda > 0$ . Then, $\omega _ { \lambda } \ \in \ x ^ { * } + s p a n ( T \ - \ x ^ { * } ) = a f f ( T )$ for any $\lambda > 0$ , while $\operatorname * { l i m } _ { \lambda \to 0 } \omega _ { \lambda } = x ^ { * }$ . Since $x ^ { * } \in T ^ { \odot }$ , therefore, there exists a $\lambda _ { o } > 0$ such that $\omega _ { \lambda } \in T ^ { \diamond }$ for every $0 < \lambda < \lambda _ { o }$ . (Yes?) $$

$$

where $\mathbf { e } \in \mathbb { R } ^ { T }$ satisfies lim $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda \to 0 \frac { | { \bf e } ( \omega _ { \lambda } ) | } { \lambda \| x \| } = 0 } \end{array}$ . The latter condition ensures that, for any $\alpha > 0$ , there is a $0 < \lambda ( \alpha ) < \lambda _ { o }$ small enough so that $| \mathbf { e } ( \omega _ { \lambda } ) | ~ <$ αλ $\| x \|$ for any $0 < \lambda < \lambda ( \alpha )$ . ## 4.2 Optimization of Concave Maps

In applications, one is frequently interested in finding the global extrema ofa given real function. Unfortunately, it is in general not so easy to determine whether a local extremum is in fact a global extremum. The case where the function to be optimized is concave (or convex), is, however, a much welcome exception. In that case the involved optimization problems are simplified by the following (informal) rule: To find the global maximum (minimum) of a concave (convex) real map, it is enough to examine the stationary points ofthat function. You are surely familiar with this principle in the case of concave or convex functions defined on an open and convex subset of a Euclidean space. We formalize it in the general case below. 

First a few preliminary observations about the optimization of concave maps.

Here is a very useful result that shows how greatly simplified the task of maximization is in the case of concave objective functions. 

## P<sub>r</sub>o<sub>p</sub>os<sub>i</sub>t<sub>i</sub>o<sub>n</sub> 10

Let T be a nonempty subset of a normed linear space X, $x ^ { * } \in T ^ { \Leftrightarrow }$ , and $\varphi \in \mathbb { R } ^ { T }$ a concave map that is Fréchet differentiable at $x ^ { * }$ . By Proposition 6, 

$$

The “only $\mathrm { i f } ^ { \dprime }$ part of the assertion is a special case of Proposition 8. 

## 5 Calculus of Variations

The main advantage ofthe generalized calculus theory we have worked out in this chapter lies, at least for economists, in its applicability to optimization problems that take place in infinite-dimensional normed linear spaces. Indeed, a variety of such problems are encountered in the daily practice of macroeconomists. Such problems are often handled by some sort of a trick that enables the analyst to use finite-dimensional techniques, or by using “optimization recipes,” the origins of which are left unexplored. By contrast, the present chapter tells us that the basic ideas behind finite- and infinite-dimensional optimization theory are identical; it is just that in the latter case we should work with Fréchet derivatives. 

Well, that’s talking the talk. In this final section ofthe text, we aim to walk the walk as well. As a case study, we take on the classical theory of calculus of variations and sketch a brief but rigorous introduction to it. We prove several necessary and sufficient conditions for (finite- and infinite-horizon) variational problems, all as easy consequences of the results of Section 4. We also consider a few applications, economic or otherwise, at the end of the discussion.<sup>34</sup> 

Before we begin, let us agree on adopting the following standard notation. 

Notation. Given any integer $n \geq 2$ , let S be a convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { n }$ with nonempty interior. For any $k \in \mathbb N ,$ , we denote by $\mathbf { C } ^ { k } ( S )$ the class of all $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( S )$ such that each partial derivative of $\varphi$ up to the kth order exists as a continuous function on $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( S )$ .<sup>35</sup> 

## 5.1 Finite-Horizon Variational Problems

We begin by laying out, in the abstract, the class of variational problems that we shall be concerned with here. 

Let $x _ { 0 }$ and $\tau$ be real numbers, and $\Omega$ a convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ . Throughout this section we assume that 

$$
\tau > 0 \quad \text { and } \quad i n t _ {\mathbb {R} ^ {2}} (\Omega) \neq \emptyset .
$$

To simplify our notation, for any $f \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ , we express the statement $^ { \alpha } ( f ( t ) , f ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) \in \Omega$ for all $0 \leq t \leq \tau ^ { \prime \prime }$ by writing $^ { \prime \prime } ( f , f ^ { \prime } ) \in \Omega . ^ { \prime \prime }$ With this convention in mind, we define 

$$
\mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ] := \{f \in \mathbf {C} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ]: f (0) = x _ {0} \text {and} (f, f ^ {\prime}) \in \Omega \},
$$

and consider this convex set as a metric subspace of ${ \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ . Of course, if $\Omega = \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , then ${ \bf C } _ { \Omega , x _ { 0 } } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ is none other than the affine manifold of ${ \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ that contains all continuously differentiable maps on $[ 0 , \tau ]$ with $f ( 0 ) = x _ { 0 }$ 

Now take any nonempty set $\mathcal { F }$ such that 

$$
\mathcal {F} \subseteq \mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ],
$$

and pick any $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , \tau ] \times \Omega )$ . In what follows, we refer to the list $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ as a smooth variational problem, and understand that this list corresponds to the following optimization problem: 

$$
\mathrm{Maximize} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t \quad \mathrm{suchthat} \quad f \in \mathcal {F},\tag{24}
$$

where we write $\varphi ( t , f , f ^ { \prime } )$ in place of the map $t \mapsto \varphi ( t , f ( t ) , f ^ { \prime } ( t ) )$ ) on [0, τ] to simplify our notation further.<sup>36</sup> (With an innocent abuse ofterminology, we will henceforth refer to the problem (24) also as a smooth variational problem.) Here $\mathcal { F }$ is called the admissible set of the problem, and $\varphi$ its Lagrangian.<sup>37</sup> 

Different choices of $\mathcal { F }$ lead to different sorts of calculus of variations problems. In particular, the smooth variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ 

where 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \{f \in \mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ]: f (\tau) = x _ {\tau} \}\tag{25}
$$

for some $x _ { \tau } \ \in \ \mathbb { R }$ is very important; this problem is referred to as a simplest variational problem. Also of interest is the so-called free-end smooth variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ , where 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ].
$$

Historically speaking, the interest in variational problems stemmed from the natural way these problems arise in Newtonian mechanics and related fields.<sup>38</sup> But of course, economists have their own reasons for studying calculus of variations. In fact, it is highly likely that you have already come across several dynamic optimization models in continuous time, so there is hardly any reason to motivate our interest in smooth variational problems. Just to be on the safe side, however, let us consider the following prototypical example. 

## E<sub>x</sub>a<sub>mpl</sub>e 11

(The Optimal Investment Problem) Consider a firm whose production technology enables it to make a profit of $P ( x )$ by using a capital stock ofx units. We assume that $P \in { \bf C } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )$ is a strictly increasing and twice continuously differentiable function with $P ( 0 ) = 0$ . The planning horizon is finite, but time is modeled continuously. So, the “time space” is $[ 0 , \tau ]$ , where 0 represents “today” and $\tau > 0$ the final date of the planning horizon. The capital accumulation of the firm through time is modeled by means of a map $f \in { \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $f \geq 0$ and $f ( 0 ) = x _ { 0 }$ , where $x _ { 0 } > 0$ stands for the initial capital stock ofthe firm, and is exogenously given. The instantaneous change in capital stock is interpreted as gross investment, which is costly. In particular, by increasing its capital stock at a given time by $\varepsilon > 0$ , the firm incurs a cost of $C ( \varepsilon )$ , where $C \in { \mathbf { C } } ^ { 2 } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )$ is strictly increasing and $C ( 0 ) = 0$ Thus, if the capital accumulation plan of the firm is $f _ { : }$ , then, at time t, the investment cost ofthe firm is $C ( f ^ { \prime } ( t ) )$ ), and hence, its total profit is found as $P ( f ( t ) ) - C ( f ^ { \prime } ( t ) )$ ). Finally, let us assume that the firm discounts the future according to the discount function $\mathfrak { d } \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $\mathfrak { d } ^ { \prime } < 0$ and $\mathfrak { d } ( 0 ) = 1$ (That is, $\mathfrak { d } ( t ) ( P ( f ( t ) ) - C ( f ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) )$ ) is the value of the time t profits from the “present” perspective of the firm.) Then, the associated optimization problem is this: 

$$
\text { Maximize } \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \mathfrak {d} (t) (P (f (t)) - C (f ^ {\prime} (t))) d t
$$

such that, $f \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ] , f ( 0 ) = x _ { 0 } { \mathrm { ~ a n d ~ } } f , f ^ { \prime } \geq 0 .$ 

This is, of course, the free-end smooth variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ where $\Omega : = \mathbb { R } _ { + } ^ { 2 }$ , and $\varphi$ is defined on $[ 0 , \tau ] \times \Omega$ by $\varphi ( t , a , b ) : = \mathfrak { d } ( t ) ( P ( a ) -$ $C ( b ) )$ ). -

LEMMA 3

Conclusion: For any $h \in \mathbf { C } _ { \Omega , x _ { 0 } } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$

and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathbf { e } ( h ) : = \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } E ( h ) ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ . By Observation 1, if h is sufficiently close to $f$ , then $\{ ( t , h ( t ) , h ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) : 0 \leq$ $t \le \tau \} \subseteq [ 0 , \tau ] \times i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ , so in this case (because , and hence $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ is convex), we have

But, since $\alpha _ { h }$ and $\beta _ { h }$ are continuous, $S$ is a compact set. (Right?) Let’s see what we got here. Suppose you are given a simplest variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ , and suppose an $f \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ , with $f ( 0 ) = x _ { 0 }$ and $( f , f ^ { \prime } ) \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ , solves the associated maximization problem. LEMMA 4
(DuBois-Reymond) For any $\tau > 0$ , if $u \in \mathbf{C}^1[0, \tau]$ satisfies $\int_0^\tau u(t) g'(t) dt = 0$ for all $g \in \mathbf{C}^1[0, \tau]$ with $g(0) = 0 = g(\tau)$ ,
then $u$ must be a constant function. 

Proof 

Let $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma : = \frac { 1 } { \tau } \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } u ( t ) d t } \end{array}$ , and define ${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { g } } } } \in { \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ by $\begin{array} { r } { g ( x ) : = \int _ { 0 } ^ { x } ( u ( t ) - \gamma ) d t } \end{array}$ Then, by the Fundamental Theorem ofCalculus, which we apply twice, and the hypothesis of the lemma, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} (u (t) - \gamma) ^ {2} d t & = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} (u (t) - \gamma) g ^ {\prime} (t) d t \\ & = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} u (t) g ^ {\prime} (t) d t - \gamma \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} g ^ {\prime} (t) d t \\ & = - \gamma (g (\tau) - g (0)) \\ & = 0. \end{array}
$$

It follows that $u = \gamma$ (Exercise A.61), and we are done.

$$

for all ${ \boldsymbol { \mathbf { \mathit { g } } } } \in { \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $g ( 0 ) = 0 = g ( \tau )$ . By hypothesis, therefore, 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} (- F (t) + w (t)) g ^ {\prime} (t) d t = 0

for all $\mathbf { g } \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $\ g ( 0 ) = 0 = g ( \tau )$ . So, by Lemma 4, $w - F$ is a constant function, that is, $\boldsymbol { w ^ { \prime } } = \boldsymbol { F ^ { \prime } } = \boldsymbol { v }$  

Here comes the punchline. 

(Euler-Lagrange) Let $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ be a simplest variational problem. $I f$ 

$$
f _ {*} \in \arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} \right\},\tag{29}

$$

Apply Observation 2, Proposition 8, Lemma 3, and Lemma 5. 

The functional equation (30) is called the Euler-Lagrange equation of the variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ and is of fundamental importance for the theory and applications ofcalculus ofvariations.<sup>42</sup> Unfortunately, in most cases this equation turns out to be a second-order differential equation, and it is hopeless to get explicit solutions out of it. Indeed, by differentiating we see that an $f \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ satisfies the Euler-Lagrange equation of $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ iff 

$$
\partial_ {2} \varphi = \partial_ {1 3} \varphi + (\partial_ {2 3} \varphi) f ^ {\prime} + (\partial_ {3 3} \varphi) f ^ {\prime \prime}.\tag{31}
$$

Despite the difficulty of solving such differential equations explicitly, one can still learn quite a bit about the nature of the solutions to the variational problem at hand by studying its Euler-Lagrange equation in implicit form. As we shall see in Sections 5.5 and 5.6, this is how the equation is used in most economic applications.<sup>43</sup> 

Theorem 1 gives us a necessary condition for an f $\mathbf { \Sigma } ^ { \prime } \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ to solve a given simplest variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ . If $\varphi$ satisfies a suitable concavity condition, then this condition is also sufficient, as we show next. 

Theorem 2 Let $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ be a simplest variational problem, and assume that $\varphi ( t , \cdot , \cdot )$ is concave for each $0 \leq t \leq \tau$ . Then, for any $f _ { * } \in \mathcal { F }$ with $( f _ { \ast } , f _ { \ast } ^ { \prime } ) \in$ $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ , (29) holds if, and only if, (30) holds. Moreover, if $\varphi ( t , \cdot , \cdot )$ is strictly concave for each $0 \leq t \leq \tau$ , then (29) (and hence (30)) can hold for at most one $f _ { * }$ . 

## Proof

Notice that $\begin{array} { r } { f \mapsto \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \varphi ( t , f , f ^ { \prime } ) d t } \end{array}$ is a concave map on ${ \mathcal F } ,$ , and apply Observation 2, Proposition 10, Lemma 3, and Lemma 5. The proof of the second claim is elementary.  

Theorem 2 stresses the importance of the Euler-Lagrange equation further. It shows that all solutions to a simplest variational problem are often characterized by the solutions to the Euler-Lagrange equation of the problem that satisfies the given boundary conditions. 

Warning. Theorem 2 gives a characterization of solutions to certain types of simplest variational problems, but it does not tell us anything about the existence of a solution to such a problem. Indeed, the Euler-Lagrange equation of a simplest variational problem may not have a solution, in which case, by Theorem 1, the involved optimization problem does not have a solution either. The “if” part of Theorem 2 says only that, under the said concavity hypothesis, provided that it exists, a solution f of the Euler-Lagrange equation (with the boundary conditions $f ( 0 ) = x _ { 0 }$ and $f ( \tau ) = x _ { \tau } )$ ), is also a solution to the involved simplest variational problem.<sup>44</sup>

f _ {*} \in \arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} \text {   and   } f (\tau) = f _ {*} (\tau) \right\},
$$

so, given that $( f _ { \ast } , f _ { \ast } ^ { \prime } ) \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ , (30) follows from Theorem 1. Moreover, by Proposition 8, Lemma 3, and integrating by parts, 

$$
\begin{array}{c} 0 = \mathsf {D} _ {\varphi , f _ {*}} (g) = \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \partial_ {2} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) g (t) d t + \partial_ {3} \varphi (\tau , f _ {*} (\tau), f _ {*} ^ {\prime} (\tau)) g (\tau) \\ - \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \frac {d}{d t} \partial_ {3} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) g (t) d t \end{array}
$$

for all $\mathbf { g } \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $g ( 0 ) = 0$ . In view of (30), we thus obtain (32). The second assertion readily follows from the computation above and Proposition 10. 

## 5.3<sup>∗</sup> More on the Sufficiency of the Euler-Lagrange Equation

In this section we revisit the sufficiency part of Theorem 2 and attempt to improve on it a bit. Here is what we have in mind. 

PROPOSITION 12
Let $[\Omega, \varphi, x_0, \tau, \mathcal{F}]$ be a simplest variational problem, and let $U, V \in \mathbf{C}^2([0, \tau] \times \mathbb{R})$ satisfy
(i) $\partial_1 U = \partial_2 V$ ;
(ii) for any $0 \leq t \leq \tau$ , the map $(a, b) \mapsto \varphi(t, a, b) + U(t, a)b + V(t, a)$ is concave on $\Omega$ .
If (30) holds for some $f_* \in \mathcal{F}$ with $(f_*, f'_*) \in int_{\mathbb{R}^2}(\Omega)$ , then (29) holds. 

(33) 

This is a genuine generalization of the first part of Theorem 2. Indeed, the latter result is obtained as a special case of Proposition 12 by setting $U = 0 = V$ 

What is the idea behind Proposition 12? (If you have solved Exercise 52, then you know the answer.) All we are doing here is to transform our original problem to the following: 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \text { Maximize } \int_ {0} ^ {1} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t + \int_ {0} ^ {1} \left(U (t, f (t)) f ^ {\prime} (t) + V (t, f (t))\right) d t \\ \text { such   that } f \in \mathcal {F}. \end{array}
$$

One can show that the condition $\partial _ { 1 } U = \partial _ { 2 } V$ implies that the second integral above is constant for any $f \in { \mathcal { F } }$ (Exercise 52.(b)). Thus an $f \in { \mathcal { F } }$ solves our original problem iff it solves the transformed problem. But, by hypothesis (ii) and Theorem 2, if (30) holds for some $f _ { * } \in \mathcal { F }$ with $( f _ { * } , f _ { * } ^ { \prime } ) \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ then $f _ { * }$ must be a solution to the transformed problem. This $f _ { * }$ , then, solves our original problem as well. 

The key step missing in this argument is supplied by the following lemma which we borrow from advanced calculus. 

LEMMA 6
For any given $\tau > 0$ and $U, V \in \mathbf{C}^{2}([0, \tau] \times \mathbb{R})$ with $\partial_{1}U = \partial_{2}V$ , there exists a $G \in \mathbf{C}^{1}([0, \tau] \times \mathbb{R})$ such that $\partial_{1}G = V$ and $\partial_{2}G = U$ . 

We shall omit the proofofthis lemma, as we do not really need $\mathrm { i t . } ^ { 4 9 }$ But it is important to note the following consequence of Lemma 6: Given any simplest variational problem $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ , if U, $V \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , \tau ] \times \mathbb { R } )$ satisfy $\partial _ { 1 } U = \partial _ { 2 } V$ , then 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \left(U (t, f (t)) f ^ {\prime} (t) + V (t, f (t))\right) d t \\ = \int_ {0} ^ {1} \frac {d}{d t} G (t, f (t)) d t = G (\tau , f (\tau)) - G (0, x _ {0}), \end{array}
$$

where G is found by Lemma 6, whence 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {1} \left(U (t, f (t)) f ^ {\prime} (t) + V (t, f (t))\right) d t = \text { constant } \quad \text { for   any } f \in \mathcal {F}.
$$

This observation hands us Proposition 12 on a silver platter. 

Proof of Proposition 12 

Define $\psi \in { \bf C } ^ { 2 } ( [ 0 , \tau ] \times \Omega )$ by $\psi ( t , a , b ) : = U ( t , a ) b + V ( t , a )$ , and let $\varphi _ { \bullet } : =$ $\varphi + \psi$ . By the preceding discussion, we have 

$$
\arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi_ {\bullet} (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} \right\} = \arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} \right\}.
$$

Thus, applying Theorem 2 to the problem $[ \Omega , \varphi _ { \bullet } , x _ { 0 } , \tau , \mathcal { F } ]$ completes the proof.  

But is Proposition 12 good for anything? That is, how are we supposed to come up with a (U, V) pair that would satisfy the requirements of this result? It is not possible to answer this query in general—the answer really depends on the kind of application one is working on—but the following corollary may provide some help. It is a nice improvement over Theorem 2. 

COROLLARY 6
Let $[\Omega, \varphi, x_0, \tau, \mathcal{F}]$ be a simplest variational problem such that there exists a map $G \in \mathbf{C}^3([0, \tau] \times \mathbb{R})$ such that, for each $0 \leq t \leq \tau$ , the map $(a, b) \mapsto \varphi(t, a, b) + \partial_2 G(t, a)b + \partial_1 G(t, a)$ is concave on $\Omega$ . If (30) holds for some $f_* \in \mathcal{F}$ with $(f_*, f_*') \in int_{\mathbb{R}^2}(\Omega)$ , then (29) holds. 

## Proof

Define $U : = \partial _ { 2 } G$ and $V : = \partial _ { 1 } G$ , and apply Proposition 12. 

In the final section of this text we will be able to use this result in an instance where Theorem 2 does not provide immediate help.

## 5.4 Infinite-Horizon Variational Problems

In the majority of economic applications, the involved variational problems arise from a dynamic model that involves an infinite time horizon. Consequently, we now turn our attention to extending the theory of calculus of variations we have exposed so far to the case of infinite-horizon variational problems. Let $x _ { 0 }$ be a real number and  a convex subset of $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ with $i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega ) \neq \varnothing$ . Denoting the statement $^ { \alpha } ( f ( t ) , f ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) \in \Omega$ for all $t \geq 0 ^ { \eta }$ as $^ { \prime \prime } ( f , f ^ { \prime } ) \in \Omega ^ { \prime \prime }$ for any $f \in \mathbf { C } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )$ , we define 

$$
\mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} (\mathbb {R} _ {+}) := \{f \in \mathbf {C} ^ {1} (\mathbb {R} _ {+}): f (0) = x _ {0} \text {   and   } (f, f ^ {\prime}) \in \Omega \}.
$$

Now consider a nonempty set ${ \mathcal { F } } \subseteq \mathbf { C } _ { \Omega , x _ { 0 } } ^ { 1 } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )$ and a map $\varphi \in \mathbf { C } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } \times \Omega )$ such that 

$$
\mathrm{(i)} \varphi \in \mathbf {C} ^ {2} (\mathbb {R} _ {+} \times \Omega);
$$

$$
\text {(ii)} \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t <   \infty \text { for   any } f \in \mathcal {F}. ^ {5 0}
$$

We refer to the list $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \mathcal { F } ]$ as an ∞-horizon smooth variational problem, and understand that this list corresponds to the following optimization problem: 

$$
\text { Maximize } \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t \quad \text { such   that } \quad f \in \mathcal {F}.\tag{34}
$$

(With an innocent abuse of terminology, we refer to the problem (34) also as an ∞-horizon smooth variational problem.) Ofparticular interest are those ∞-horizon smooth variational problems where 

$$
\mathcal {F} = \mathbf {C} _ {\Omega , x _ {0}} ^ {1} (\mathbb {R} _ {+}).\tag{35}
$$

The following is sometimes called the Rounding-OffCorners Lemma. 

LEMMA 7
Let $[\Omega, \varphi, x_0, \mathcal{F}]$ be an $\infty$ -horizon smooth variational problem. Let $\mathcal{X}$ stand for the class of all $f \in \mathbf{C}(\mathbb{R}_+)$ such that
(i) $f(0) = 0$ ;
(ii) $f'_+$ and $f'_-$ exist everywhere on $\mathbb{R}_{++}$ ;
(iii) there exists a $t_o > 0$ such that $f|_{\mathbb{R}_+ \setminus \{t_o\}} \in \mathbf{C}^1(\mathbb{R}_+ \setminus \{t_o\})$ and $(f(t), f'(t)) \in \Omega$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}_+ \setminus \{t_o\}$ .
Then $\sup \left\{ \int_0^\infty \varphi(t, f, f') dt : f \in \mathcal{F} \right\} = \sup \left\{ \int_0^\infty \varphi(t, f, f') dt : f \in \mathcal{X} \right\}$ . 

Exercise 60 Prove Lemma 7. 

We can now easily derive the Euler-Lagrange equation for ∞-horizon smooth variational problems. The idea is simply to use Theorem 1 for any truncation of the problem at hand, and then utilize Lemma 7 to “patch $\mathrm { u p } ^ { \dprime }$ what we find in these truncations. 

## Theorem 3

Let $[ \Omega , \varphi , x _ { 0 } , \mathcal { F } ]$ be an ∞-horizon smooth variational problem, and le $f _ { * } \in \mathcal { F }$ satisfy $( f _ { * } , f _ { * } ^ { \prime } ) \in i n t _ { \mathbb { R } ^ { 2 } } ( \Omega )$ . If 

$$
f _ {*} \in \arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} \right\},\tag{36}
$$

then, 

$$
\partial_ {2} \varphi (t, f _ {*} (t), f _ {*} ^ {\prime} (t)) = \frac {d}{d t} \partial_ {3} \varphi (t, f _ {*} (t), f _ {*} ^ {\prime} (t)) \quad \text {for all} t > 0,
$$

while the converse also holds when $\varphi ( t , \cdot , \cdot )$ is concavefor each $0 \leq t \leq \tau$ 

## Proof

Assume that (36) holds. In view of Theorem 1, it is enough to show that, for any $\tau > 0$ 

$$
f _ {\tau} | _ {[ 0, \tau ]} \in \arg \max \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \varphi (t, f, f ^ {\prime}) d t: f \in \mathcal {F} _ {\tau} \right\},
$$

where $f _ { \tau } : = f _ { * } | _ { [ 0 , \tau ] }$ and $\mathcal { F } _ { \tau } : = \{ f \in \mathbf { C } _ { \Omega , x _ { 0 } } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ] : f ( \tau ) = f _ { * } ( \tau ) \}$ }. (Right?) To derive a contradiction, suppose the latter statement is false, that is, there exist a $\tau > 0$ and an $h \in \mathcal { F } _ { \tau }$ such that $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \varphi ( t , h , h ^ { \prime } ) d t > \int _ { 0 } ^ { \tau } \varphi ( t , f _ { \tau } , f _ { \tau } ^ { \prime } ) d t . } \end{array}$ Define $\mathbf { g } \in \mathbf { C } ( \mathbb { R } _ { + } )$ as 

$$
g (t) := \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} h (t), & \text { if } 0 \leq t \leq \tau \\ f _ {*} (t), & \text { otherwise } \end{array} \right..
$$

Then, by Lemma 7, we have 

$$
\int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \varphi (t, f _ {*}, f _ {*} ^ {\prime}) d t \geq \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \varphi (t, g, g ^ {\prime}) d t > \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} \varphi (t, f _ {*}, f _ {*} ^ {\prime}) d t,
$$

which is absurd. The proof of the second assertion is left to the reader. 

## 5.5 Application: The Optimal Investment Problem

We consider the optimal investment problem introduced in Example 11 under the following assumptions: 

ASSUMPTION (A)
(i) $P \in \mathbf{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ is a bounded function with $P(0) = 0$ , $P' > 0$ , $P'' \leq 0$ and $P_{+}'(0) = \infty$ .
(ii) $C \in \mathbf{C}^{2}(\mathbb{R}_{+})$ , $C(0) = 0 = C'(0)$ , $C|_{\mathbb{R}_{++}}' > 0$ and $C'' > 0$ .
(iii) $\mathfrak{d} \in \mathbf{C}^{2}[0, \tau]$ , $\mathfrak{d}(0) = 1$ , $\mathfrak{d} > 0$ and $\mathfrak{d}' < 0$ . 

Let us first look into the case where the firm has a target level of capital stock at the end of the planning horizon, say $x _ { \tau } ~ > ~ 0$ , so the problem it faces is: 

$$
\text { Maximize } \int_ {0} ^ {\tau} \mathfrak {d} (t) (P (f (t)) - C (f ^ {\prime} (t))) d t
$$

such that 

$$
f \in \mathbf {C} ^ {1} [ 0, \tau ], f (0) = x _ {0}, f (\tau) = x _ {\tau} \text {and} f ^ {\prime} \geq 0.
$$

It can be shown that, under the premises of $( \mathsf { A } )$ , this problem admits a solution $f \in { \bf C } ^ { 1 } [ 0 , \tau ]$ with $f , f ^ { \prime } \gg 0$ . (We omit the proof.) Since the map $( a , b ) \mapsto P ( a ) - C ( b )$ is strictly concave on $\mathbb { R } ^ { 2 }$ , this solution is unique, and by Theorem 1, it is characterized by the Euler-Lagrange equation of the problem and its boundary conditions. It follows that the optimal capital accumulation planf satisfies 

$$
P ^ {\prime} (f (t)) = - \frac {\mathfrak {d} ^ {\prime} (t)}{\mathfrak {d} (t)} C ^ {\prime} (f ^ {\prime} (t)) - C ^ {\prime \prime} (f ^ {\prime} (t)) f ^ {\prime \prime} (t), \quad 0 <   t <   \tau .
$$

We can interpret this differential equation as follows. $P ^ { \prime } ( f ( t ) )$ is the time t marginal benefit of the firm that corresponds to the capital accumulation plan $f$ . On the other hand, $- { \frac { \mathfrak { d } ^ { \prime } ( t ) } { \mathfrak { d } ( t ) } }$ is the relative discount rate at time t, so $- \frac { \mathfrak { d } ^ { \prime } ( t ) } { \mathfrak { d } ( t ) } C ^ { \prime } ( f ( t ) )$ corresponds to forgone (subjective) interest on the money invested in capital. Finally, the term $C ^ { \prime \prime } ( f ^ { \prime } ( t ) ) f ^ { \prime \prime } ( t )$ can be interpreted as the capital gains or losses that may have occurred through time. All in all, the Euler-Lagrange equation in the present case is a dynamic formulation of the principle that the firm has to invest in such a way that its marginal benefit and marginal cost at any given point in time are equal to each other. 

Suppose we now omit the condition $f ( \tau ) = x _ { \tau }$ , and hence consider the problem of the firm as a free-end smooth variational problem. In that case, Corollary 5 tells us that we must have $C ^ { \prime } ( f ^ { \prime } ( \tau ) ) = 0$ in the optimum. Since $C ^ { \prime } | _ { \mathbb { R } _ { + + } } > 0$ , this is possible if $f ^ { \prime } ( \tau ) = 0$ . So we learn that additional investment at the final period τ should be zero in the optimum. (This makes sense, of course, as there is no time left to make use of an investment undertaken at τ.) 

Incidentally, this observation shows that if we assumed $C ^ { \prime } ( 0 ) > 0$ in $( \mathrm { A . i i } )$ (as would be the case if C was a linear function, for instance), then there would be no solution to the free-end variational problem of the firm
